newsitem.title: INDIA: INDIAN DLR FORWARD PREMIUMS END HIGHER ON RBI MOVE.
newsitem.headline: INDIAN DLR FORWARD PREMIUMS END HIGHER ON RBI MOVE.

text.p: Forward premiums ended up in volatile trade on Tuesday following a decision by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Monday to allow foreign funds to hedge their investments in Indian debt, bank dealers said.
"Forward premiums opened up and were fairly erratic today," said the chief dealer at a public sector bank.
He said forward premiums closed five to six paise higher on sentiment following RBI's Monday announcement.
"July dollars opened today at a premium of 1.67 rupees compared with the previous close of 1.57," said a foreign bank chief dealer.
"Premiums then drifted lower before rising again."
December, April and July delivery dollars were active, dealers said.
The six month annualised forward premium closed the day at 4.54 percent compared to the previous close of 4.14 percent.
Sunil Sharma, chief forex dealer at ANZ Grindlays Bank, said actual FII investment in debt would be at $100-$150 million.
"Given a steady rupee, you won't expect all of this to be covered," Sharma said. "I would think it reasonable to expect hedging of about 25 percent of this amount."
FIIs were allowed to invest in Indian debt earlier this year and leading European and American investment banks have committed over $2.0 billion for Indian debt.
But few funds have actively begun investing because of several problems, including the unavailability of forward cover.
The spot rupee was stable at 35.71/72, dealers said.
The rupee saw a high of 35.7100 and a low of 35.7150.
The RBI was in the market, buying an estimated $30-$40 million, dealers said, but its intervention did not have much impact on the exchange rate, dealers said.
